I'm looking at the documents, and I just thought I'd note what this hack is and isn't capable of. Lets not be too alarmist here. This isn't a hack that lets the CIA just hack into your network through your firewall from half way across the world. They need physical or wireless access to your router.

Physical Access: They sneak in through your window and plug into your router with a laptop then try and login to your router using the default password. If you never changed your router login password (that is something different than your wifi password), they just use that and are in and can install the corrupt firmware. If you did change your wireless router password, they are still locked out. Keep in mind, that if they got physical access, it doesn't even matter. They could put anything they want in your environment to intercept your data, and this hack would just be one option.

Wireless Access only: Ok, so they can't get in, but are parked outside in a plumbing truck within wifi range of your router. Step 1, they still need to get onto your wifi. My understanding is that now a days a hacker who knows what they are doing can get through WEP/WPA pretty easily now, so assume they crack that in a Jiffy. They are now wirelessly connected to your network. They try and connect to your router using the default password. If you never changed your router login password (that is something different than your wifi password), they just use that and are in and can install the hacked firmware. If you did change your wireless router password, they are still locked out. At this point they could do a brute force attempt on the password, so if your password is "abc123" you are still fucked. In theory, if your password is weak, or if they sat out there long enough they could get in this way.

Now even if they did get wireless access and you didnt change your password, if your particular router model doesn't allow WLAN Firmware updates, they are still shit out of luck and are going to have to go back to plan B through the window.

TLDR; There isn't much to be concerned about here even if your router is on the list. If you are paranoid, go change your wireless router's admin password to something long and complex, as long as the CIA hasnt already been outside your house and hacked into your router, you will be immune.

If the CIA is going to show up outside your house, them hacking your wireless router is probably the least of your concerns.

I disagree with a few of these points. The docs list this as the typical means of infection: "...either using the Claymore tool or via a supply chain operation"

We don't yet know what 'Claymore' is, but a 'supply chain operation' would be the CIA implanting it either with complicit vendors or by intercepting devices in-transit before they're sold. All-in-all, that's not all that far fetched but probably not what is happening for most people.

You often don't need physical or wireless access to compromise a router. Typically, this is when the devices don't protect against something called cross-site request forgery (CSRF). These attacks originate from a site on the Internet, which calls back to your router to make some sort of state-changing action on the device. Often you need to be logged into your router for this to work, because the browser will include your session information along with any requests, even from external locations. That's not always the case though... I've found issues in recent history that don't require you to be logged into the device, although generally it has to be chained together with other vulnerabilities (like debug functionality left on the device, which happens quite often). CSRF is hard to fully explain, but if you want to read up more about it, check out this.

Just to speculate, 'Claymore' could be something like an 0-day in, for instance, the lighttpd web server. You know, a web server developed by a handful of people on a volunteer basis and used on probably a majority of these sorts of devices.
